title: How many fit, and the copycat game
summary: Divide fractions by asking how many fit, watch money grow on its own growth, and discover the copy trick that wins the two pile game.
materials: counters or coins for the pile games

problems.prompt: A drummer starts soft and doubles every bar: 1 beat, then 2, then 4, then 8. How many beats land in the fifth bar?
explanation: Find the rule: each bar holds double the bar before it.
The fourth bar holds 8 beats, so the fifth holds double that.
Double 8 is 16.
problems.useAgain: when each step of a pattern is made from the step before it by the same one move.
hints: Say what happens from one bar to the next: what one move keeps repeating?
Apply that same move to the fourth bar.
problems.socraticHint: Is this pattern adding the same amount each bar, or doing something else each bar?

variant.prompt: A drummer doubles every bar: 3 beats, then 6, then 12, then 24. How many beats land in the fifth bar?

problems.prompt: A song fades out by halving: 32 claps in a bar, then 16, then 8. If the halving keeps going, how many claps are in the fifth bar?
explanation: Find the rule: every bar holds half the bar before it.
After 8 comes half of 8, which is 4, in the fourth bar.
The fifth bar holds half of 4, so 2 claps.
problems.useAgain: when a pattern shrinks by the same split each step and you ride it down.
hints: Each bar is built from the bar before it. What is the one move?
Work out the fourth bar first, then build the fifth from it.
problems.socraticHint: Doubling built the drummer's pattern up. What is this pattern's move, and how are the two moves related?

variant.prompt: A song fades out by halving: 48 claps in a bar, then 24, then 12. How many claps are in the fifth bar?

problems.prompt: Your drum bars come in four sizes: 1 beat, 2 beats, 4 beats and 8 beats. Using each size at most once, which set of bars adds up to exactly 11 beats?
explanation: Two symbols are enough: the doubling sizes 1, 2, 4 and 8 are the whole toolkit, one recipe per count.
Start from the biggest size that fits: 8 fits inside 11, leaving 3.
4 is too big for the leftover 3. 2 fits, leaving 1, and 1 finishes the job.
8 plus 2 plus 1 is 11. This in or out recipe is exactly how your fingers and your LEDs spell numbers this week.
problems.useAgain: when you spell a number out of doubling pieces, on fingers, on LEDs, or anywhere on and off live.
hints: Try the biggest size first: does 8 fit inside 11, and what is left over?
Spell the small leftover using only the sizes you have not used yet.
problems.socraticHint: Why does taking the biggest size that fits never get you stuck here?

variant.prompt: Same four bar sizes: 1, 2, 4 and 8 beats, each used at most once. Which set of bars adds up to exactly 13 beats?

problems.prompt: Claps land on beats 1, 2, 4, 7 and 11, with the gap growing by one each time. Which beat number gets the next clap?
explanation: Find the rule by looking at the gaps: from 1 to 2 is a gap of 1, then gaps of 2, then 3, then 4.
The gaps climb by one each time, so the next gap is 5.
11 plus 5 is 16.
problems.useAgain: when the pattern hides in the gaps between the numbers instead of in the numbers themselves.
hints: Write down the jump between each pair of neighbours.
The jumps themselves make a pattern. Ride it one more step.
problems.socraticHint: If the numbers themselves refuse to show a rule, where else in the row could a rule hide?

variant.prompt: Claps land on beats 2, 3, 5, 8 and 12, with the gap growing by one each time. Which beat number gets the next clap?

problems.prompt: A pattern repeats forever: clap, clap, snap, clap, clap, snap. What is the 12th sound?
explanation: The pattern loops in blocks of 3 sounds: clap, clap, snap.
12 splits into 4 whole blocks of 3 with nothing left over.
No leftover means the 12th sound closes a block, and every block closes with snap.
problems.useAgain: when a repeating loop makes a far away position easy to find from the leftover after dividing.
hints: How many sounds make one full block of the pattern?
Divide 12 by the block length and look hard at what is left over.
problems.socraticHint: Which counting positions always land on a block's last sound?

variant.prompt: A pattern repeats forever: clap, snap, snap. What is the 10th sound?

problem.prompt: You light the top row and the left column of the 5 by 5 matrix, a bracket shape hugging the top left corner. Then you turn the whole micro:bit a half turn, so it hangs upside down. Which picture do the lit pixels make now? Sketch the grid on graph paper and spin the paper if you want to check your head against your hands.
options: The top row and the right column are lit
The bottom row and the left column are lit
The top row and the left column are lit
The bottom row and the right column are lit
explanation: Turn it in your head: a half turn is a spin of the whole grid, not a mirror flip.
A half turn sends every pixel to the spot straight across the center. The top row lands on the bottom row, and the left column lands on the right column.
So the lit bracket ends up hugging the opposite corner: the bottom row and the right column.
Check one pixel to be sure: the old top left corner travels to the bottom right corner. That is exactly where the bottom row meets the right column.
problem.useAgain: when a picture or a board is spun all the way around and you need to know where each part lands.
hints: A half turn is a spin, not a mirror: the picture goes upside down and swaps sides at the same time.
Follow just one corner pixel of the bracket and see where the spin carries it.
problem.socraticHint: Where does the very center pixel of the grid go in a half turn, and why is it the only one that stays put?

figure.alt: A 5 by 5 grid of pixels with the top row and the left column filled in, making a bracket that hugs the top left corner. The whole grid is then turned a half turn. The turned grid is not shown.

variant.prompt: No picture this time, so build it in your head: on the 5 by 5 matrix you light the bottom row and the left column, a bracket hugging the bottom left corner. You turn the whole micro:bit a half turn. Which picture do the lit pixels make now? Sketch the grid on graph paper, shade the bracket, and spin the paper before you choose.
options: The bottom row and the right column are lit
The top row and the right column are lit
The bottom row and the left column are lit
The top row and the left column are lit

steps.title: Divide by a fraction: how many fit

problems.prompt:
Wren solved how many quarter-cup scoops fit in 5 cups, which is 5 divided by 1/4.
Line 1: Dividing by a fraction means flipping it and multiplying instead.
Line 2: Flip 1/4 to get 4/1, which is just 4.
Line 3: Multiply 5 by 4.
Line 4: 5 times 4 is 9, so 9 quarter-cup scoops fit in 5 cups.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Lines 1 through 3 are correct: dividing by a fraction means flipping it and multiplying, and 5 times 4 is the right move.
Line 4 is wrong: 5 times 4 is 20, not 9.
That 9 looks like 5 plus 4 instead of 5 times 4.
How many fit: dividing 5 cups by quarter-cup scoops asks how many quarter-cups sit inside 5 whole cups.
The correct answer is 20 quarter-cup scoops fit in 5 cups.
problems.useAgain: when a fraction division's flip step is right but the final multiplication still needs checking on its own.
hints: Do not assume any line is correct just because the ones before it look fine. Recompute each line yourself.
Flip and multiply: only the fraction gets flipped, and then the flipped fraction multiplies the other number.
problems.socraticHint: If flipping and multiplying is the right method, does this working actually flip the fraction and then multiply?

variant.prompt:
Deja solved how many third-cup scoops fit in 4 cups, which is 4 divided by 1/3.
Line 1: Dividing by a fraction means flipping it and multiplying instead.
Line 2: Flip 1/3 by swapping the top and bottom of the 4 instead, giving 1/4.
Line 3: Multiply 1/3 by 1/4.
Line 4: 1/3 times 1/4 is 1/12, so 1/12 of a third-cup scoop fits in 4 cups.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: Which of these equals 2/3 divided by 1/6?
explanation: How many fit: the question asks how many 1/6 pieces fit inside 2/3.
Cut everything into sixths first: 2/3 is the same as 4/6.
Inside 4/6, a piece of size 1/6 fits exactly 4 times.
Flip and multiply agrees: 2/3 times 6 is 12/3, which is 4. Multiplying without flipping is the trap that lands on 1/9.
problems.useAgain: when both fractions can be cut into the same size slices so the division becomes a simple count.
hints: Rewrite 2/3 in sixths before you do anything else.
Once both fractions speak in sixths, just count how many pieces fit.
problems.socraticHint: If you owned 2/3 of a pizza and handed out slices of 1/6 each, what count is the division really asking you for?

variant.prompt: Which of these equals 3/5 divided by 1/10?

problems.prompt: Which of these equals 3/5 divided by 2/5?
explanation: Both fractions already speak in fifths, so ask how many times 2 fifths fits into 3 fifths.
2 fits into 3 one whole time, with 1 fifth left over.
The leftover fifth is half of a piece of size 2 fifths, so the answer is 1 1/2.
Flip and multiply agrees: 3/5 times 5/2 is 15/10, which is 1 1/2. Flipping the wrong fraction is the trap that lands on 2/3.
problems.useAgain: when the bottoms already match and dividing the fractions is just dividing the tops.
hints: The bottoms match, so compare only the tops: how many times does 2 fit into 3?
Measure the leftover against the size of the piece you are dividing by, not against a whole.
problems.socraticHint: The leftover fifth is not a whole piece of size 2 fifths. What fraction of one of those pieces is it?

variant.prompt: Which of these equals 5/8 divided by 3/8?

problems.prompt: Do not compute anything yet. Just by comparing sizes, which division lands on an answer bigger than 1?
explanation: How many fit answers this with no arithmetic. The answer beats 1 exactly when the amount you start with is bigger than the piece you divide by.
2/3 is bigger than 1/2, so at least one whole 1/2 piece fits inside it. That answer is bigger than 1.
1/2 is smaller than 3/4, and 1/4 is smaller than 1/2, so in both of those not even one whole piece fits.
problems.useAgain: when you want to predict the size of an answer before computing it, as a check on your work.
hints: In each division, compare the two fractions: which of the pair is bigger?
If the piece is smaller than the amount you start with, at least one whole piece fits.
problems.socraticHint: What has to be true about the two fractions for at least one whole piece to fit?

variant.prompt: Do not compute anything yet. Just by comparing sizes, which division lands on an answer bigger than 1?

problems.prompt: A ribbon is 7/8 of a meter long. One bow takes 1/4 of a meter of ribbon. How many bows worth of ribbon do you have? Answer as a mixed number.
explanation: This asks how many 1/4 pieces fit inside 7/8.
Cut everything into eighths: 1/4 is 2/8, and the ribbon is 7/8.
2 fits into 7 three whole times, with 1 eighth left over, and that leftover is half of a piece of size 2/8.
So the ribbon holds 3 1/2 bows worth. Flip and multiply agrees: 7/8 times 4 is 28/8, which is 3 1/2.
problems.useAgain: when a real length or amount gets shared out in fraction sized pieces and a leftover shows up.
hints: Rewrite 1/4 in eighths so both lengths speak the same slice size.
Count the whole pieces first, then measure the leftover against one piece.
problems.socraticHint: The leftover eighth of a meter is not a whole bow. What fraction of one bow is it?

variant.prompt: A ribbon is 5/6 of a meter long. One bow takes 1/3 of a meter. How many bows worth of ribbon is that? Answer as a mixed number.

problems.prompt: You put 100 dollars in the family bank. It grows by 10 percent every year, and each new year grows the whole pile, including last year's growth. Chart it on graph paper as you go: one bar for the start, then one bar after each year. How many dollars sit in the bank after 2 years?
explanation: Money snowball: the growth itself starts growing.
Year one: 10 percent of 100 is 10, so the pile becomes 110.
Year two: 10 percent of 110 is 11, not 10, because the pile is bigger now.
110 plus 11 is 121 dollars. Draw it on your chart and watch the yearly jumps get taller.
problems.useAgain: when money or anything else grows by a percent of its new size each round, not by a flat amount.
hints: Work out year one first: what is 10 percent of 100, and how big is the pile after it lands?
Year two grows from the year one pile, not from the starting 100.
problems.socraticHint: Why is the second jump bigger than the first, when the percent never changed?

variant.prompt: You put 100 dollars in the family bank at 10 percent a year, each year growing the whole pile. Chart each year on graph paper as you go. How many dollars after 3 years?

problems.prompt: Two banks offer deals on your 100 dollars. Bank A adds a flat 10 dollars every year. Bank B grows your pile by 10 percent every year. After 3 years, which pile is bigger?
explanation: Bank A climbs the same stair every year: 110, then 120, then 130.
Bank B snowballs: 110, then 121, then 133.10.
They tie after the first year, and every year after that the snowball pulls ahead, because it grows on its own growth. Doubling fingers and doubling money are the same fast forward trick.
problems.useAgain: when you compare a flat gain against a percent gain over more than one round.
hints: Write both piles year by year, side by side.
Find the year the two piles stop matching, then ask why they split there.
problems.socraticHint: In year one the two deals hand you the very same 10 dollars. What is different about where year two's growth is measured from?

variant.prompt: Same two banks, same 100 dollars: Bank A adds a flat 10 dollars a year, Bank B grows the pile 10 percent a year. After exactly 1 year, which pile is bigger?

steps.title: Angles that split unevenly, and telling equally likely from not

problems.prompt: An isosceles triangle has two equal base angles of 70 degrees each. What is the third angle, in degrees?
explanation: All three angles still add to 180 degrees, equal sides or not.
Add the two equal base angles: 70 plus 70 is 140.
180 minus 140 is 40 degrees.
problems.useAgain: when a triangle has two equal angles and only the third, different one is missing.
hints: Two of the angles are equal here; add them together first.
Subtract that sum from 180 for the third angle.
problems.socraticHint: Does a triangle having two equal angles change how much its three angles add up to?

variant.prompt: An isosceles triangle has two equal base angles of 55 degrees each. What is the third angle, in degrees?

problems.prompt: Two angles on a straight line are in the ratio 2 to 3. What is the smaller angle, in degrees?
explanation: The ratio 2 to 3 splits the line's 180 degrees into 5 equal parts.
180 divided by 5 is 36 degrees per part.
The smaller angle is 2 parts: 2 times 36 is 72 degrees.
problems.useAgain: when a straight line's 180 degrees is split between two angles in a given ratio.
hints: Add the two numbers in the ratio to find how many equal parts make up 180 degrees.
Find the size of one part, then multiply by the smaller ratio number.
problems.socraticHint: If the two angles are shared in a 2 to 3 ratio, how many equal parts is the full 180 degrees split into?

variant.prompt: Two angles on a straight line are in the ratio 1 to 2. What is the smaller angle, in degrees?

problems.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled. True or false: rolling a 4 is just as likely as rolling any other single number on the die.
explanation: A fair die has six equal-sized faces, so no number is favored over another.
Every single number, 1 through 6, has exactly the same 1 out of 6 chance.
That is what makes it fair, not that every number comes up the same amount every time you roll.
problems.useAgain: when deciding whether every outcome of a random device has an equal chance, by checking whether the physical shares are equal.
hints: Are all six faces of a fair die the same size?
Equal-sized faces mean every number has the same chance.
problems.socraticHint: Does a die need to actually land on every number the same number of times in ten rolls to be fair?

variant.prompt: A spinner has a bigger green region and a smaller red region. True or false: landing on green is just as likely as landing on red.

problems.prompt: A spinner is divided into 3 equal-sized sections: red, blue and green. True or false: landing on red is twice as likely as landing on blue.
explanation: Equal-sized sections always carry equal chances, no matter their color.
Red and blue are the same size here, so they share the exact same 1 out of 3 chance.
One would only be twice as likely if its section were twice as big.
problems.useAgain: when comparing the chances of two outcomes by comparing the physical size of their sections, not their color or order.
hints: Are the red and blue sections the same size or different sizes?
Equal sizes always mean equal chances.
problems.socraticHint: What would have to be true about the sizes of the sections for one color to be twice as likely as another?

variant.prompt: A spinner has one large red section (half the circle) and two small equal sections for blue and green. True or false: landing on red is twice as likely as landing on blue.

figure.alt: White to move. The white queen on a5 faces a lone black rook on a7, with the black king too far away to help it.

problems.prompt: White to move. One black piece has no defender. Which move wins it for free?
explanation: The black rook on a7 has no other piece guarding it.
The white queen already lines up with a7 along the open file.
Qxa7 simply takes the rook, and nothing can take the queen back.
problems.useAgain: when an enemy piece sits on a line your piece already controls, with nothing defending it.
hints: Check every black piece: does anything else in black's army protect it?
Look at which of your own pieces already lines up with that undefended piece.
problems.socraticHint: If you took that piece right now, could black take your piece back?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move captures the undefended black bishop?

figure.alt: White to move. A white rook on d1 faces a black bishop alone on d5.
White to move. Black's king on g8 is boxed in by pawns on f7, g7 and h7, with a white rook on a1.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move gives checkmate?
explanation: Black's king on g8 is boxed in by its own three pawns.
Ra8 lands on the open back rank right beside the king, with nothing in the way.
The king has nowhere to run and nothing can capture the rook, so it is mate.
problems.useAgain: when a king is boxed in by its own pawns and the back rank is open.
hints: Look at the king's own pawns. Do they leave it any square to step to?
Find the rook move that reaches the very last row next to the king.
problems.socraticHint: Why can none of black's pawns capture or block a rook arriving on the back row?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move gives checkmate?

figure.alt: White to move. Black's king on b8 is boxed in by pawns on a7, b7 and c7, with a white rook on h1.
White to move. A white knight on d3 faces two undefended black rooks on a6 and c6.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move attacks two black rooks at once?
explanation: A knight jumping to b4 lands on a square that attacks both a6 and c6 at the same time.
Both black rooks sit there with nothing defending them.
Black can only save one rook, so white wins the other.
problems.useAgain: when one knight move can land on a square that attacks two enemy pieces at once.
hints: Find a square the knight can reach that touches two black pieces at the same time.
Check both a6 and c6 from that square.
problems.socraticHint: If black can only make one move, which rook will still be standing after it?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move attacks two black rooks at once?

figure.alt: White to move. A white knight on c4 faces two undefended black rooks on c6 and g6.
White to move. A white bishop on f1 faces a black knight on c6, with the black king on e8 behind it on the same diagonal.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move pins the black knight to its king?
explanation: The black king sits on e8 and the knight on c6 is on the very same diagonal.
Bb5 lines the bishop up with the knight and the king behind it, so the knight cannot move.
A pinned piece cannot run away, so white can attack it again next.
problems.useAgain: when an enemy piece and its own king share a straight line your piece can reach.
hints: Look for a line that already runs through the knight and the king behind it.
Find the bishop move that lands on that same line.
problems.socraticHint: If the knight tried to move away right now, what would happen to its king?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move pins the black knight to its king?

figure.alt: White to move. A white bishop on a4 faces a black knight on g6, with the black king on h7 behind it on the same diagonal.

problems.prompt: The pile game: on your turn, take any number of counters from one pile, and whoever takes the last counter wins. Two piles sit at 6 and 6, and it is the other player's turn. True or false: whatever amount they take from one pile, you can always take the same amount from the other pile.
explanation: Copycat pairing: answer their move with its twin on the other pile.
The piles are equal, so whatever they take from one pile, the untouched pile holds at least that many.
Say they take 4 from the first pile. The second pile still has all 6, so taking 4 from it is always allowed.
After your copy the piles are equal again, ready for the next copy.
problems.useAgain: when a game position is balanced and mirroring the other player keeps it balanced.
hints: They must take from one pile only, so the other pile is untouched when your turn comes.
Compare the most they could take with what the untouched pile still holds.
problems.socraticHint: Could they ever take more counters from one pile than the other pile contains?

variant.prompt: Same game, but the piles sit at 7 and 4, and it is the other player's turn. True or false: whatever amount they take from one pile, you can always take the same amount from the other pile.

problems.prompt: Piles of 5 and 3, your turn, last counter wins. Which move sets up the copycat plan?
options: Take all 5 from the pile of 5
explanation: The copycat plan needs twin piles sitting in front of the other player.
Taking 2 from the pile of 5 leaves 3 and 3, perfectly balanced, and now every move they make has a twin waiting for you.
The other moves hand the game away. Leaving 5 and 1, or leaving a single pile, lets a sharp player balance things against you or simply take everything.
problems.useAgain: when the piles are unequal and one move can turn them into twins.
hints: Count the difference between the two piles.
Which single move makes the two piles hold the same amount?
problems.socraticHint: After your move it is their turn. Why does the copycat want the piles equal at exactly that moment?

variant.prompt: Piles of 6 and 2, your turn, last counter wins. Which move sets up the copycat plan?
options: Take all 6 from the pile of 6

problems.prompt: The piles start equal, the other player goes first, and you copy every move on the other pile. True or false: the very last counter of the game must end up in your hand.
explanation: After every one of your copies the piles are equal again, so the other player always faces twin piles.
The piles shrink every round, so the game cannot go on forever.
Twin piles can never both be emptied by one move on one pile, so the other player can never take the final counter.
The move that empties the table is always a copy, and every copy is yours. That is why the plan can never lose.
problems.useAgain: when you want to know who wins from a balanced position, not just what the next move is.
hints: After each of your copies, describe exactly what the other player is looking at.
Can one move on one pile ever empty two twin piles at once?
problems.socraticHint: The game ends when the table is empty. Can the table become empty right after one of their moves, if the piles were twins before it?

variant.prompt: Piles start at 8 and 8, the other player goes first, and you copy every move. True or false: the other player can somehow grab the very last counter.

problems.prompt: Piles of 10 and 7, your turn, last counter wins. You start the copycat plan. How many counters does your first move take?
explanation: The copycat plan starts by making the piles twins.
10 and 7 differ by 3, so take 3 from the bigger pile.
That leaves 7 and 7, and from there every move they make has a copy waiting for you.
problems.useAgain: when the first move of a balancing plan is just the difference between the two piles.
hints: The move must come from the bigger pile. Why can the smaller one not work?
Find how far apart the two piles are.
problems.socraticHint: What single number measures how unbalanced the piles are right now?

variant.prompt: Piles of 12 and 5, your turn. You start the copycat plan. How many counters does your first move take?

problems.prompt: Piles of 9 and 9. The other player takes 4 from one pile, and you copy on the other pile. How many counters are left on the table in total after your copy?
explanation: Start with 9 plus 9, which is 18 counters on the table.
Their move removes 4, and your copy removes another 4, so the round removes 8 in all.
18 minus 8 leaves 10, sitting as twin piles of 5 and 5.
problems.useAgain: when you track a game by the total on the table and every full round removes double one move.
hints: Count what is on the table before anyone moves.
A full round removes their counters and your matching counters together.
problems.socraticHint: Every copy round removes an even number of counters. What does that keep true about the two piles?

variant.prompt: Piles of 7 and 7. The other player takes 3 from one pile, and you copy on the other. How many counters are left on the table in total after your copy?

problems.prompt: Three piles now: 2, 2 and 1, your turn, last counter wins. Which move keeps you safe?
explanation: Taking the lone 1 leaves piles of 2 and 2 with the other player to move: exactly the balanced spot the copycat loves.
From 2 and 2 you copy their every move, and the last counter is yours.
Check the other moves with your counters: they leave 2, 1 and 1, or 2 and 1 instead. From both spots a sharp player balances the piles against you and copies you to the end.
problems.useAgain: when an extra pile appears and one move can turn the game back into a balanced two pile game.
hints: You already know which two pile positions are safe to hand to the other player.
Which move leaves the other player staring at twin piles?
problems.socraticHint: The lone pile of 1 is the odd one out. What happens to the shape of the game the moment it disappears?

variant.prompt: Three piles: 3, 3 and 2, your turn, last counter wins. Which move keeps you safe?

problems.prompt: True or false: the copycat trick by itself hands you the winning move in every pile setup there is.
explanation: Set out piles of 1, 2 and 3 and try it. No move makes twins with nothing left over, and a careful other player beats you however you copy.
So some setups resist the copycat. They are not unbeatable, they just keep a deeper secret.
The full secret is built from two machine parts. One is binary, which you built this very week. The other part arrives in week 3.
The lock opens in week 9, and you will earn the secret instead of being told it.
problems.useAgain: when a trick that wins one game meets a bigger game and you test honestly whether it still works.
hints: Set out piles of 1, 2 and 3 with real counters and play both sides yourself.
Copying needs a twin to copy onto. Do three different piles always offer one?
problems.socraticHint: When a position beats you over and over, what is the difference between there is no trick and I have not found the trick yet?

variant.prompt: True or false: in the two pile game, copycat thinking finds the winning move whenever the two piles are unequal.

steps.title: Explain it in writing
steps.prompt: Write, in your own words, why the copycat plan on twin piles never runs out of copies, and why the very last counter always lands in your hand.

steps.title: Explain it out loud
steps.prompt: Record yourself explaining why taking the lone pile of 1 is the safe move from piles of 2, 2 and 1, and what your plan is for the rest of that game.
